thread.title: Apple's Share Cycle And Tim Cook's Buyback Effect - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) | Seeking Alpha

author: Zvi Bar
title: Apple's Share Cycle And Tim Cook's Buyback Effect - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Apple’s ( AAPL ) 2019 may end up looking like 2013 and 2016, both of which provided investors with excellent opportunities to acquire shares in the first half of those years. This recent decline supports an apparent recurring cycle affecting Apple share valuations that I believe is consistently related to the company’s product line and emerging market demographics. Like the prior instances, this should present a better than average long-term investment opportunity.
There are also different accompanying forces this time due to the addition of Berkshire Hathaway as a major holder and the significant stock buyback plan increase that Apple instituted in 2018. Each of these is likely to be a continuing supportive feature that is unlikely to go away any time soon.
Buffett Buying, Holding & Probably Buying Again According to Berkshire Hathaway’s 13-Fs ( most recent here ), it purchased around 240 million shares of Apple stock between 2016 and the end of the first quarter of 2018 at prices between about $90 and $180. Of that 240 million, about 130 million were acquired before Q1 2018 and therefore acquired at prices below around $145, and some of the other 110 million shares were probably not much higher priced. Berkshire’s cost basis on Apple at the end of 2017 was about $126 per share.
Berkshire added only 522,802 shares of Apple in Q3 of Apple in the last reported quarter, Q3 of 2018, down from around 12 million in Q2 2018, indicating Buffett significantly slowed down or stopped buying Apple shares at or around the $180, and possibly considerably lower. Information on Q4 is not yet available, and Q1 2019 info will not be available for months, though Buffett may make a comment after Berkshire reports earnings. Nonetheless, it appears probable that Berkshire will continue to hold its current shares and acquire more significant quantities of new Apple shares when at a nicer price. I think Apple is within his nicer price range here. Reporting will tell.
Tim Cook’s Massive Buyback Probably Will Continue Take a look at what Apple did in 2018 (source: Apple)
Between Q1 of 2016 and Q1 of 2018, Apple bought back, each quarter, somewhere between six and eleven billion dollars worth of shares. Starting in Q2 of 2018, the company massively increased the buyback and has since acquired between $19.4 and $23.5 billion per quarter, roughly tripling the average quarterly buyback in dollar terms. At the same time, Apple kept its total quarterly dividend obligation roughly stable, even though the dividend per share went up about 28 percent in the past two years.
I believe Tim Cook will continue this recent stock buyback trajectory, because that was always the plan and also it would look bad to turn back right now. Also, the company has the cash, and shares are back at about the price where this new level of buying back started anyway. If anything, the buyback is likely to fine an accompanying accelerated component added. Similarly, the dividend is safe, and is likely to be increased this year, and probably by between ten and twenty percent.
Apple Cycles Through Similar Issues Some things seem to happen to apple. Maybe it is because all their stuff is proprietary and expensive, but also excellent and popular. In any case, the company has gone through similar fluctuations in the past, and this time may conclude in a comparable manner. I believe it will conclude when Apple announces new buyback and dividend terms, and continue through the coming device cycle.
In 2013, Apple shares started the year having sustained considerable declines in late 2012, and they remained weak through the first two quarters, at which point they turned around. Apple also declined at the end of 2015, and remained weak at the start of 2016, but they turned around during the second quarter of 2016. If this year ends up being anything like those, this recent decline may continue further, or stall at this recent range for a while, but it should turn around in the coming months. Passive Buying Will Continue Apple is still one of the largest companies in the world, and among the largest constituents of the S&P 500 (about 3.1%) and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (about 4.3%). Apple should capture passive investment dollars in relative proportion to its market size, which continues to be significant. Apple also sustains selling when the broader market sells off. This broader market selling may be what keeps or pushes Apple oversold. If the broader market sells off, Apple should likely only acquire more shares. Berkshire and value investors may do the same, and when broader market buying rebounds, it will find a reduced float from which to acquire Apple shares.
Conclusion Market sentiment and Apple chart history indicate the stock is oversold and may remain oversold for the next few months. Possible catalysts exist in the form of Apple's probable buyback plan and dividend payout increase announcements, rumors of new products and Berkshire acquisition updates.
